analysis.one_liner: Replaces the graduated federal income tax with a flat 15% rate on all income, with small per-person and per-child deductions.
analysis.headline: The Flat Tax Rate Act, a one-sentence bill to tax all income at 15%, died without a vote after being referred to the Ways and Means Committee; it had no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have thrown out the current income tax brackets, which tax higher incomes at higher rates, and replaced them with a single 15% tax on everyone's income. Each taxpayer would get a deduction — $10,000 for a single person, $20,000 for a married couple, plus $3,000 per child under 18 — and everything above that would be taxed at 15%. Because people in the top brackets pay far more than 15% today, the biggest winners would be the highest earners, while families who benefit from today's lower bottom rates and credits could end up paying more.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most, since a flat 15% rate is far below the current top rates. Moderate and lower-income households would lose the preferential low rates and credits they receive today, offset only by the fixed deductions.

how_it_helps.text: It replaces all current income tax brackets with a single 15% rate, which would lower the tax bill of anyone currently in a bracket above 15% — overwhelmingly high-income households.
It simplifies filing: everyone pays the same rate on income above a fixed deduction ($10,000 single, $20,000 joint, $3,000 per child under 18).

analysis.who_pays: Lower- and middle-income taxpayers, who would lose the low rates and credits they get under the current progressive structure, and the Treasury would lose revenue from the top brackets.

drawbacks.text: Replacing the current progressive rate structure with one 15% rate would cut taxes most for the highest earners while removing the lower rates and credits that low- and middle-income households rely on, raising taxes on many working families.
The exemptions are modest — $10,000 for a single filer, $20,000 for a couple, $3,000 per child — which does not compensate for losing the current code's deductions and credits.

The bill is three sentences long and contains no detail on how it interacts with existing credits, payroll taxes, or the deficit, and no plan to replace the revenue the current progressive code raises.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The appeal is simplicity: one rate and a small standard deduction would make filing easier and end phase-outs and special breaks. But the cost is a large tax cut for the highest earners paid for by higher taxes on low- and middle-income families, since the current code's higher top rates and credits — the parts the bill removes — are what shield ordinary households. As written, the bill did not offset its revenue loss, and it received no support beyond its single sponsor before the Congress ended.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, got no cosponsors, and died there when the Congress ended with no vote ever taken.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 11, 2014 — about three weeks before the 113th Congress ended — and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee.
The committee took no action; the only recorded actions are introduction and referral, and the bill never received a vote.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The current progressive income tax structure was left in place; no household's taxes changed. Had it passed, high earners would have been the main beneficiaries.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing progressive tax code stands

for.name: Rep. Steve Stockman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the final weeks of the 113th Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split was ever tested in a vote.

industries.note: Moving from top marginal rates near 40% to a flat 15% would deliver the largest tax cut to the highest earners, while the loss of progressive rates and credits would raise taxes on many working families.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and financial services industry
industries.note: A radically simpler code would reduce demand for complex tax planning and filing services in the long run, though a bill that never advanced had no practical effect.
